subtopic_detail: Timing of delivery for asymptomatic placenta praevia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternal foetal medicine clinic. A 33 year old para 1 at 34 weeks has known placenta praevia with the placental edge covering the internal os by 22 mm on transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks. She has had no bleeding episodes throughout pregnancy. Her first birth was a caesarean at term for foetal distress.

On examination she is well with no abdominal pain, no bleeding per vaginum and normal foetal movements. Speculum has not been performed. Foetal heart rate is 148 on cardiotocography.

Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Bloods show haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 234 x10^9/L, blood group A positive, antibody screen negative. Estimated foetal weight is on the 60th centile with normal amniotic fluid index. She has been counselled to attend immediately if any bleeding occurs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82/min; BP 118/74 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C; FHR 148/min
data_table.Examination: No abdominal pain; no bleeding; normal foetal movements; CTG normal
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: placenta covers os by 22 mm at 32 weeks; Hb 118 g/L; platelets 234 x10^9/L; group A+ antibody negative; EFW 60th centile; normal AFI
data_table.History: Para 1 previous LSCS at term for foetal distress; asymptomatic through pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Await spontaneous labour and perform vaginal delivery given the absence of bleeding to date with continuous cardiotocography and immediate caesarean if bleeding occurs
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is not safe with a placenta covering the internal os by more than 10 mm; catastrophic haemorrhage occurs at labour onset and elective caesarean is required (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section at 39 plus 0 weeks with a magnetic resonance imaging scan to exclude placenta accreta first after multidisciplinary team discussion
options.rationale: Waiting until 39 weeks exposes the woman to a substantial risk of spontaneous labour with catastrophic haemorrhage; the earlier window at 36 to 37 plus 6 weeks is chosen for this reason (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section between 36 plus 0 and 37 plus 6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity
options.rationale: The RANZCOG guidance for asymptomatic placenta praevia is to plan elective caesarean section between 36 plus 0 and 37 plus 6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids, balancing prematurity risk against unplanned haemorrhage from spontaneous labour (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Admit now for continuous cardiotocographic monitoring until spontaneous delivery with cross match samples sent for transfusion readiness
options.rationale: Continuous inpatient monitoring in the absence of bleeding or contractions has no benefit and prolongs admission; outpatient monitoring with clear return advice is standard (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Perform external cephalic version at 36 weeks and then await spontaneous vaginal delivery with continuous cardiotocography and inpatient monitoring after the attempt
options.rationale: External cephalic version is contraindicated in placenta praevia because manipulation of the uterus may precipitate placental bleeding (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

explanation.summary: Placenta praevia with the placental edge covering the internal cervical os by more than 20 mm on transvaginal ultrasound after 32 weeks mandates elective caesarean section. The RANZCOG guidance is to plan the caesarean between 36 plus 0 and 37 plus 6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids because the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage with spontaneous labour is high while foetal maturity gains beyond 37 weeks are marginal. External cephalic version is contraindicated because it may precipitate haemorrhage. Ongoing outpatient monitoring with clear return advice is preferred over prolonged inpatient stay in the absence of bleeding or contractions.
key_points: Placenta covering os by more than 10 mm needs elective caesarean.
Delivery window 36 plus 0 to 37 plus 6 weeks with corticosteroids.
External cephalic version is contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: For asymptomatic placenta praevia the RANZCOG delivery window is deliberately early at 36 to 37 plus 6 weeks; a single course of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly 24 hours apart gives foetal lung maturity while pre empting spontaneous labour.

sources.label: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

subtopic_detail: Surgical choice for tubal ectopic after contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old para 0 at 7 weeks of amenorrhoea with 3 days of right iliac fossa pain. She had a left salpingectomy 3 years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for 8 months and would like future fertility preserved if possible.

On examination she has mild right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding but no peritonism. Speculum shows a closed cervix and no bleeding.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Serum beta hCG is 3200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a right adnexal complex mass measuring 32 by 28 mm with a yolk sac visible; no foetal cardiac activity is seen; there is a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 118/70 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding; no peritonism; closed cervix; no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 3200 IU/L; Hb 128 g/L; TVUS empty uterus, right adnexal mass 32 x 28 mm with yolk sac, no foetal cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas free fluid
data_table.History: Para 0 at 7 weeks; left salpingectomy 3 years ago for ruptured ectopic; trying to conceive 8 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer methotrexate 50 mg per square metre intramuscularly and follow up with serial beta hCG measurements
options.rationale: Methotrexate would preserve the tube pharmacologically, however with an adnexal mass containing a yolk sac and pain there is a significant failure rate; more importantly this is the woman's only remaining tube and preserving its function is a priority, which favours a laparoscopic conservative approach given operative access and beta hCG below the RANZCOG surgical threshold (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Perform laparoscopic right salpingectomy given the higher risk of persistent trophoblast with tube conservation
options.rationale: Salpingectomy removes future spontaneous conception potential from that tube; in a woman with only one tube left the balance of persistent trophoblast risk against loss of tubal function favours salpingostomy (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Observe with expectant management and repeat beta hCG in 48 hours before deciding on intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for asymptomatic women with a small mass, no free fluid and a falling beta hCG below 1500 IU/L; this presentation with pain, free fluid and a mass with a yolk sac needs active management (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Perform laparoscopic salpingostomy on the right tube with serial beta hCG follow up until zero
options.rationale: The woman has had a contralateral salpingectomy so the right tube is her only remaining tube; salpingostomy preserves tubal patency and future intrauterine fertility potential and is preferred over salpingectomy when tubal preservation matters, with serial beta hCG follow up to detect persistent trophoblast (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Perform diagnostic laparoscopy with wedge cornual resection to preserve the fimbrial end of the tube
options.rationale: Cornual resection is used for interstitial or cornual ectopics, not for a mid tubal adnexal ectopic; it damages the myometrium and is not indicated for a typical ampullary ectopic (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

explanation.summary: In a haemodynamically stable woman with a tubal ectopic and a contralateral salpingectomy, salpingostomy on the remaining tube preserves future intrauterine fertility and is preferred over salpingectomy despite a modestly higher rate of persistent trophoblast, which is managed with serial beta hCG monitoring. The RANZCOG surgical threshold of a beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L pushes towards salpingectomy in a woman with a normal contralateral tube, but where the contralateral tube is absent the calculus flips towards conservation. Methotrexate is a reasonable alternative when the mass is small, there is no pain and beta hCG is below 5000 IU/L, but requires reliable follow up. Expectant management is reserved for asymptomatic small ectopic pregnancies with a falling beta hCG below 1500 IU/L.
key_points: Only remaining tube: salpingostomy preferred over salpingectomy.
beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L is the RANZCOG surgical threshold when a normal contralateral tube exists.
Serial beta hCG follow up detects persistent trophoblast.
explanation.pearls: Whenever an ectopic occurs after a contralateral salpingectomy, the surgical default flips from salpingectomy to salpingostomy because loss of the last tube ends spontaneous intrauterine conception potential.

subtopic_detail: Augmentation of labour after previous caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birthing unit. A 32 year old para 1 at 40 plus 3 weeks was admitted 5 hours ago in spontaneous labour. Her previous birth was a lower segment caesarean section 2 years ago for breech presentation at term with a normal wound and no interval infection. She was counselled antenatally on trial of labour after caesarean and consented to it.

She is contracting 2 in 10 for 40 seconds with adequate strength. Her cervix is 5 cm dilated, fully effaced, station minus 1, with cephalic presentation. Amniotomy 2 hours ago was clear. She has an epidural in situ working well. Her partogram shows no cervical change over the last 2 hours.

Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C. Foetal heart rate on cardiotocography is 140 with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88/min; BP 122/78 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.9 C; FHR 140/min normal variability
data_table.Examination: Contracting 2 in 10 for 40 sec; cervix 5 cm, fully effaced, station -1, cephalic; membranes ruptured 2 h ago; clear liquor
data_table.Progress: No cervical change over 2 hours; epidural in situ
data_table.History: Previous LSCS 2 years ago for breech; consented VBAC; no interval infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a Foley catheter for mechanical cervical dilation without pharmacological augmentation to reduce uterine rupture risk and continue continuous cardiotocography with reassessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Mechanical cervical ripening with a Foley catheter is used for cervical ripening before labour, not to augment established labour that has stalled; oxytocin augmentation is the standard approach here (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Give a single dose of vaginal prostaglandin E2 3 mg to accelerate the labour and continue continuous cardiotocography with reassessment at 4 hours with continuous cardiotocography and reassessment at 4 hours
options.rationale: Vaginal prostaglandins are contraindicated for the augmentation of labour after previous caesarean due to a threefold increase in uterine rupture risk (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Recommend immediate repeat caesarean section as the safest option given the failure to progress after discussing the risks and benefits with her and her partner in detail
options.rationale: Failure to progress for 2 hours in the active phase does not meet the definition of failure of labour after caesarean; a trial of oxytocin augmentation with careful monitoring is the standard first step (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Continue expectant management with intermittent auscultation and reassess cervix in 4 hours and offer analgesia adjustment as required by the epidural service
options.rationale: Intermittent auscultation is not appropriate in a woman with a previous caesarean because subtle changes in the foetal heart rate are an early sign of uterine rupture; continuous cardiotocography is required (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Commence intravenous oxytocin infusion titrated to contractions of 4 in 10 with continuous cardiotocography and one to one midwifery care with escalation to the on call obstetric consultant if needed
options.rationale: A woman with a previous single low transverse caesarean, inadequate contractions in the active phase and no cervical progress over 2 hours may have oxytocin augmentation with careful titration and continuous cardiotocography; the RANZCOG guidance is oxytocin is not contraindicated after previous caesarean but rupture risk is increased and monitoring must be continuous with one to one midwifery care (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

explanation.summary: In a woman attempting a trial of labour after caesarean with inadequate contractions and no cervical progress in the active phase, intravenous oxytocin augmentation is not contraindicated but requires careful titration with continuous cardiotocography and one to one midwifery care because the risk of uterine rupture is around 0.5 to 1 percent. Vaginal prostaglandins are contraindicated for augmentation after previous caesarean due to a threefold rupture risk. Intermittent auscultation is inadequate because subtle changes in the foetal heart trace are the earliest sign of scar rupture. Repeat caesarean is reserved for failure of the trial or for foetal or maternal compromise, not for a single 2 hour period of arrest.
key_points: Oxytocin can be used to augment labour after previous caesarean with continuous CTG.
Vaginal prostaglandins are contraindicated after previous caesarean.
Continuous cardiotocography detects early signs of uterine rupture.
explanation.pearls: After a previous single low transverse caesarean the baseline uterine rupture rate is around 0.5 percent and rises to around 1 percent with oxytocin augmentation, still allowing a monitored trial of labour to proceed.

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection in first episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community early intervention team. A 19 year old university student is referred by his general practitioner with a 6 week history of paranoid ideas that his housemates are recording him, hearing voices commenting on his actions, and social withdrawal. He is a rugby player who cares about his fitness. His mother has hypothyroidism.

On mental state examination he is guarded but cooperative, with thought disorder and second person auditory hallucinations. He has no suicidal ideation and no aggressive plans. His weight is 78 kg, height 182 cm, waist circumference 82 cm.

Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.2 percent (less than 5.7), total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, ECG QTc 402 ms. He is antipsychotic naive and consents to treatment. He asks specifically about medication that will not cause weight gain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Weight 78 kg; height 182 cm; waist 82 cm; guarded; thought disorder; second person auditory hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.2%; total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L; ECG QTc 402 ms
data_table.History: Antipsychotic naive; concerned about weight gain

lead_in: Which antipsychotic is the most appropriate first line choice?

options.text: Aripiprazole 10 mg orally in the morning, titrated according to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden among first line atypicals with minimal weight gain and prolactin elevation; the RANZCP schizophrenia guideline lists it among first line agents in first episode psychosis, and it aligns with the patient's expressed priority (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg orally at night, titrated according to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Olanzapine has efficacy in first episode psychosis but has the highest weight gain and metabolic burden of the atypicals and is generally avoided in a metabolically clean young man who has raised the concern (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg orally at night, titrated to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol are not first line in first episode psychosis because of higher extrapyramidal side effects that increase the risk of medication discontinuation (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Clozapine 25 mg orally at night with a weekly full blood count for monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics due to its haematological and metabolic risks; it is not a first line choice in a treatment naive patient (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Quetiapine 300 mg orally at night, titrated to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Quetiapine has moderate weight gain and sedation and is not as effective as other atypicals at doses under 400 mg per day; it is not the preferred first line agent for a metabolically conscious young man with first episode psychosis (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis is managed with an atypical antipsychotic chosen for its side effect profile rather than for a specific mechanism of action because the atypicals have similar efficacy in this setting. Aripiprazole is often chosen for young metabolically clean patients because it has the lowest weight gain and prolactin elevation among the first line agents. Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden and is avoided when weight or diabetic risk is a concern. Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics.
key_points: Aripiprazole: lowest weight gain and prolactin among first line atypicals.
Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden.
Clozapine reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after 2 adequate trials.
explanation.pearls: In first episode psychosis the atypicals have equivalent efficacy but very different side effect profiles; matching the drug to the patient's own priorities (metabolic, sedation, sexual side effects) improves adherence and long term outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring and renal decline
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team reviewing a 58 year old woman with bipolar I disorder well controlled on lithium carbonate 750 mg orally at night for the last 22 years. Her lithium levels have been between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L on 3 monthly monitoring.

She is euthymic with no recent mood episodes and remains at work part time. She has no polyuria or polydipsia and no thirst. She takes ibuprofen occasionally for arthritis and has recently started perindopril for hypertension. Weight 78 kg, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg.

Her latest bloods show lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), creatinine 118 micromol/L rising from 92 micromol/L 6 months earlier (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min per 1.73 m squared (was 68 mL/min per 1.73 m squared), sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 within normal limits, calcium corrected 2.62 mmol/L (2.10-2.60).

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); creatinine 118 micromol/L (was 92) (45-90); eGFR 48 (was 68) mL/min/1.73 m^2; Na 140 mmol/L; K 4.3 mmol/L; TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free T4 within normal limits; corrected calcium 2.62 mmol/L (2.10-2.60)
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte for 22 years; recent perindopril; occasional ibuprofen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Immediately stop the lithium and switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily to prevent further renal decline and arrange nephrology and psychiatry follow up within the week
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium discontinuation risks relapse of bipolar illness within weeks and switching without discussion is inappropriate; renal decline is managed by review of contributing drugs and dose reduction with continued monitoring under specialist input (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose, cease ibuprofen and review the perindopril in liaison with the general practitioner, and refer to nephrology with follow up bloods in 2 to 4 weeks to assess trajectory
options.rationale: The falling estimated glomerular filtration rate reflects contributions from long term lithium, ibuprofen and perindopril; the guideline recommends dose reduction to the lowest effective concentration, review of nephrotoxic co medication in collaboration with the general practitioner and nephrology referral once the eGFR is below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the lithium dose to keep the level between 0.8 and 1.0 mmol/L to guarantee ongoing prophylactic efficacy and repeat urea, electrolytes and creatinine measurements in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Higher lithium concentrations increase the risk of long term nephrotoxicity and thyroid dysfunction; in a euthymic patient the aim is to use the lowest effective concentration rather than the highest tolerated (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily to control fluid balance and improve renal function and repeat lithium levels in 5 to 7 days to monitor for a rise
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics reduce renal clearance of lithium and precipitate toxicity; they should not be added without careful review of the lithium dose (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Take no action because the lithium level is within the therapeutic range and repeat renal function in 12 months and continue with routine 3 monthly monitoring as previously arranged
options.rationale: A drop in eGFR of 20 mL/min per 1.73 m squared over 6 months is significant and requires active management; delayed review of 12 months risks irreversible renal decline (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

explanation.summary: Long term lithium therapy is associated with a progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate; the risk rises with duration, high concentrations, episodes of toxicity and concurrent nephrotoxic drugs. When the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared the RANZCP guidance is to reduce the dose to the lowest effective concentration, review co medication such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and thiazide diuretics, and consider nephrology referral. Thyroid dysfunction and hyperparathyroidism are also long term concerns and require targeted testing. Discontinuation is a specialist decision and requires slow tapering over months with alternative mood stabilisation planned.
key_points: eGFR below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared triggers dose review and specialist input.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and thiazides increase lithium levels.
Slow taper over months if discontinuation is required.
explanation.pearls: A creatinine rise of even 20 micromol/L in a stable lithium patient warrants review of nephrotoxic co medication because the combination of lithium plus non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus ACE inhibitor can accelerate irreversible renal decline within months.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of SSRI discontinuation from depressive relapse
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34 year old woman who is 5 days into stopping paroxetine 20 mg daily after 14 months of treatment for a first episode of major depression. She stopped abruptly against advice when she felt too well to continue. She reports dizziness, brain zaps, and irritability over the last 3 days.

On assessment she has no anhedonia, her sleep is normal, appetite normal, energy has been high, and she has been enjoying her hobbies. There is no suicidal ideation and no hopelessness. She scores 4 on the PHQ-9.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. No focal neurological findings. She is worried that her illness is returning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: No anhedonia; sleep normal; appetite normal; enjoying hobbies; no suicidal ideation; PHQ-9 score 4; no focal neurology
data_table.History: Stopped paroxetine 20 mg after 14 months, 5 days ago; dizziness, brain zaps, irritability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose depressive relapse, increase paroxetine to 40 mg daily and add cognitive behavioural therapy referral
options.rationale: Relapse presents with a return of core depressive symptoms over weeks, not with dizziness and brain zaps within days of stopping; the pattern here fits discontinuation syndrome and increasing to a higher dose is not warranted (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure that the symptoms will resolve within a few days without any medication and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Untreated paroxetine discontinuation typically lasts 1 to 3 weeks and can be severe; simply waiting is unpleasant for the patient and misses the opportunity to teach appropriate tapering practice (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch immediately to fluoxetine 20 mg to bridge the discontinuation because of its long half life
options.rationale: Bridging with fluoxetine may be considered when a patient cannot tolerate re exposure to the original drug; it is not the first step when the pragmatic option of restarting the original drug and tapering is available (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Explain that these are discontinuation symptoms, restart paroxetine at the usual dose and taper over 6 to 8 weeks
options.rationale: The onset within days of stopping short half life SSRI, presence of dizziness and paraesthesia and absence of core depressive symptoms is classical SSRI discontinuation syndrome; restarting at the previous dose and tapering over 6 to 8 weeks resolves symptoms and avoids conflating them with relapse (Source: TG Psychotropic; RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Refer urgently to psychiatry as the symptoms are likely a paroxetine hypersensitivity reaction
options.rationale: Discontinuation symptoms are the expected pharmacological response, not a hypersensitivity reaction; hypersensitivity would present with rash, angioedema or serotonin syndrome, none of which is present (Source: TG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: SSRI discontinuation syndrome typically appears within 1 to 3 days of stopping a short half life SSRI such as paroxetine, includes dizziness, paraesthesia, brain zaps, irritability and flu like symptoms, and resolves within 1 to 3 weeks. It is distinguished from depressive relapse by the timing, absence of core depressive symptoms, and rapid response to restarting the drug. Restarting at the usual dose and tapering over 6 to 8 weeks is the standard approach. Fluoxetine bridging is an option if re exposure to the original drug is not tolerated.
key_points: Onset within days of stopping suggests discontinuation, not relapse.
Paroxetine and venlafaxine have the shortest half lives and cause the most severe discontinuation.
Taper over 6 to 8 weeks after restarting.
explanation.pearls: A PHQ-9 under 5 with dizziness, brain zaps and paraesthesia within a week of stopping paroxetine reads as discontinuation, not relapse; restart the drug and taper over 6 to 8 weeks rather than escalating dose.

stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 32 year old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking around 3 grams of amitriptyline in a suicide attempt. She is drowsy but rousable. She has a background of depression and no known cardiac history.

On examination she is warm and dry with dilated pupils and a mildly dry mouth. There are no focal neurological signs. She responds to verbal stimuli and follows commands slowly.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C. GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118, QRS 128 ms, QTc 468 ms, terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. Venous blood gas pH 7.32, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. Point of care glucose 5.6 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.1 C; GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; dilated pupils; dry mouth; no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 118; QRS 128 ms; QTc 468 ms; aVR terminal R 4 mm; VBG pH 7.32, HCO3 18 mmol/L; glucose 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.History: 3 g amitriptyline 90 min ago; depression; no cardiac history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g orally and observe on the ward for 4 hours with cardiac monitoring and reassess the ECG at each hour and repeat the ECG at each hour
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is not routinely given beyond 1 to 2 hours of ingestion because gastric absorption is largely complete; more importantly the ECG changes require immediate sodium bicarbonate rather than delayed decontamination (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Give flumazenil 0.2 mg intravenously and reassess the airway and level of consciousness and prepare for benzodiazepines if any seizure activity develops
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in tricyclic overdose; it may precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses and unmask sodium channel toxicity (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Perform gastric lavage and give a magnesium sulfate 2 g intravenous infusion over 20 minutes with airway protection and cardiac monitoring in a resuscitation area
options.rationale: Gastric lavage is not standard care beyond the first hour and carries aspiration risk in a drowsy patient; magnesium is for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and not first line without arrhythmia (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Give phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous loading dose over 20 minutes to prevent seizures and admit to a monitored bed with continuous cardiac telemetry throughout
options.rationale: Phenytoin is contraindicated in tricyclic overdose because it shares sodium channel blockade and worsens cardiotoxicity; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 100 mL of 8.4 percent intravenous bolus and admit to a monitored resuscitation bay with continuous cardiac telemetry and repeat blood gas monitoring hourly
options.rationale: A QRS above 100 ms and terminal R wave in aVR indicate significant sodium channel blockade and predict cardiovascular collapse and seizures in tricyclic overdose; sodium bicarbonate at 1 to 2 mmol/kg (100 mL of 8.4 percent for a 70 kg adult) narrows the QRS and reduces arrhythmia risk (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre; TG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose produces sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR and risk of cardiovascular collapse and seizures, plus anticholinergic effects. A QRS above 100 ms or a terminal R wave in aVR of at least 3 mm is an indication for a sodium bicarbonate bolus of 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeated to keep the QRS narrow and to buffer acidosis. Benzodiazepines are used for seizures; phenytoin is contraindicated because it worsens the sodium channel blockade. Activated charcoal is only useful within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion and gastric lavage is not routine due to aspiration risk.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms or aVR terminal R at least 3 mm: give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg.
Benzodiazepines for seizures; phenytoin is contraindicated.
Charcoal only within 1 to 2 hours; lavage is not routine.
explanation.pearls: A tricyclic overdose with QRS above 160 ms carries a 50 percent risk of ventricular arrhythmia, so give the first sodium bicarbonate bolus at the bedside as soon as the ECG is seen rather than waiting on blood gas results.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and treatment considerations
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 28 year old accountant with lifelong difficulty concentrating that has worsened since starting a demanding new role 6 months ago. He describes forgetting deadlines, restlessness, losing keys and interrupting others in meetings. His school reports at age 8 described him as fidgety and easily distracted. He drinks 4 standard drinks per week and does not use recreational drugs.

On mental state examination he is engaging, mildly restless in his chair, and thought content shows no depressive or anxious cognitions. He denies suicidal ideation and there is no history of mania. He drives to work daily and has no motor vehicle accidents in the last 3 years.

Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. He completed an Adult ADHD Self Report Scale returning 5 of 6 positive items in Part A. Full blood count, thyroid function, iron studies and ECG are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72/min; BP 118/74 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Engaging; mildly restless; no depressive or anxious content; no suicidality; no mania history
data_table.Investigations: ASRS Part A: 5 of 6 positive; FBC, TFT, iron studies and ECG within normal limits
data_table.History: Lifelong difficulty concentrating, worse for 6 months; childhood school reports positive; 4 standard drinks per week; no drug use; drives daily; no crashes 3 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for structured diagnostic assessment and formal management plan
options.rationale: The clinical picture is suggestive of adult ADHD with childhood onset symptoms and functional impairment; Australian practice is a formal assessment by a psychiatrist or paediatrician to confirm diagnosis, exclude co morbidity and initiate stimulant treatment under authority arrangements (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline; Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence a trial of dexamfetamine 5 mg orally twice daily and review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: In Australia stimulant medication for ADHD requires an authority from a psychiatrist or paediatrician; the general practitioner cannot initiate it and must refer for formal assessment (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline; PBS authority conditions).

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and commence sertraline 50 mg daily
options.rationale: There are no core anxiety symptoms; treating a presumed anxiety disorder without evidence risks missing the underlying ADHD and delays appropriate care (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline).

options.text: Advise him to stop driving until an ADHD diagnosis is confirmed and stimulants are commenced
options.rationale: Australian fitness to drive standards do not require driving cessation while awaiting ADHD assessment in a patient with no crashes and no significant impairment behind the wheel (Source: Austroads assessing fitness to drive).

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing as the necessary first line diagnostic investigation
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing is not required for ADHD diagnosis in most cases; the diagnosis is clinical, based on symptom criteria plus childhood onset and functional impairment (Source: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD is diagnosed clinically on the presence of childhood onset symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity impulsivity, functional impairment across two or more domains, and exclusion of alternative causes; screening tools such as the Adult ADHD Self Report Scale support but do not replace formal assessment. In Australia the initiation of stimulant medication requires an authority prescription by a psychiatrist or paediatrician. Non stimulant options such as atomoxetine and guanfacine are second line. Fitness to drive is preserved unless there is evidence of significant impairment or repeated at fault crashes.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical with childhood onset and functional impairment.
Stimulant initiation requires psychiatrist or paediatrician authority in Australia.
Neuropsychological testing is not required for the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: For a working adult with functional impairment and a positive ASRS Part A, refer directly to a psychiatrist or paediatrician; only they can start stimulant medication under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme authority rules in Australia.

sources.label: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clozapine clinic. A 44 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg orally at night for 8 years with stable full blood counts and complete symptomatic remission. He identifies as Aboriginal and his baseline neutrophil count has averaged 1.9 x10^9/L over the last year, which is his benign ethnic neutropenia pattern already registered with the local clozapine monitoring service.

He is well with no fever, no sore throat, and no infective symptoms. Physical examination is unremarkable. He has not started any new medications in the last month.

Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Today's full blood count shows neutrophils 1.3 x10^9/L (2.0-8.0), white cell count 3.6 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 232 x10^9/L. Previous count 5 days ago was neutrophils 1.9 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: No fever; no sore throat; no infective symptoms; asymptomatic
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.3 x10^9/L (2.0-8.0); WCC 3.6 x10^9/L; Hb 138 g/L; platelets 232 x10^9/L; 5 days ago neutrophils 1.9 x10^9/L
data_table.History: Aboriginal; benign ethnic neutropenia registered; clozapine 400 mg for 8 years; no new medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step under Australian clozapine monitoring guidance?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and admit for haematology assessment and arrange psychiatric review to plan alternative maintenance treatment
options.rationale: Under the benign ethnic neutropenia framework the alert threshold is a neutrophil count under 1.0 x10^9/L rather than the general 1.5 x10^9/L cut off; a count of 1.3 x10^9/L does not mandate immediate cessation and haematology admission (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring guidance; RANZCP clozapine consensus).

options.text: Continue clozapine and repeat the full blood count within 2 days, monitoring for infective symptoms and arrange psychiatric review to plan any change to the maintenance regimen
options.rationale: The registered benign ethnic neutropenia protocol allows continued clozapine while the neutrophil count remains at or above 1.0 x10^9/L, with an increased monitoring frequency to at least twice weekly counts and a clinical review for infective symptoms; a count of 1.3 x10^9/L in an asymptomatic patient meets that requirement (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring guidance; RANZCP clozapine consensus).

options.text: Add lithium 250 mg orally three times daily to increase the neutrophil count and mask the drop and repeat the full blood count in 2 weeks to assess the neutrophil response
options.rationale: Lithium is sometimes used to raise neutrophil counts but is not first line and does not replace protocol monitoring; adding lithium in an otherwise stable patient introduces long term risk without an evidence based indication (Source: RANZCP clozapine consensus).

options.text: Give filgrastim 300 micrograms subcutaneously and continue clozapine at the same dose and increase the frequency of full blood count monitoring for the next 2 weeks
options.rationale: Granulocyte colony stimulating factor is used for clozapine associated neutropenia below 0.5 x10^9/L or with fever, not for a mild reduction in an asymptomatic patient with benign ethnic neutropenia already registered (Source: RANZCP clozapine consensus).

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 200 mg orally at night to lower the marrow burden and repeat the full blood count in 3 to 5 days to check for recovery
options.rationale: Clozapine induced agranulocytosis is not dose dependent; halving the dose does not reduce the risk and risks psychiatric relapse (Source: RANZCP clozapine consensus).

explanation.summary: The Australian clozapine monitoring services use a standard neutrophil alert threshold of 1.5 x10^9/L below which the drug is stopped, however a benign ethnic neutropenia protocol lowers the alert to 1.0 x10^9/L when a registered lower baseline has been documented. In a registered patient with an asymptomatic neutrophil count between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L, clozapine may continue with increased monitoring frequency and clinical review for infective symptoms. Granulocyte colony stimulating factor and lithium are not first line and are reserved for specific circumstances. Dose reduction does not reduce agranulocytosis risk because the toxicity is idiosyncratic rather than dose dependent.
key_points: Standard neutrophil alert threshold on clozapine is 1.5 x10^9/L.
Benign ethnic neutropenia lowers the alert to 1.0 x10^9/L if registered.
Clozapine agranulocytosis is idiosyncratic, not dose dependent.
explanation.pearls: A registered benign ethnic neutropenia protocol on Clopine Connect allows clozapine to continue with a neutrophil count between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L, provided monitoring frequency doubles and any fever or infective symptom triggers immediate cessation and haematology review.

subtopic_detail: Bipolar disorder in pregnancy and mood stabiliser choice
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 30 year old para 0 at 6 weeks of pregnancy. She has bipolar I disorder with two previous manic episodes requiring inpatient care. She has been well on lithium carbonate 1000 mg orally at night for the last 4 years with a serum level of 0.7 mmol/L. She and her partner planned this pregnancy and she wishes to continue her medication if it is safe to do so.

She is euthymic on mental state examination with future oriented planning and no perceptual disturbance. She takes no other medications.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 2.6 mIU/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, eGFR greater than 90 mL/min per 1.73 m squared. She asks whether her medication should change during pregnancy given what she has read about Ebstein anomaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 118/74 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic; future oriented; no perceptual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 2.6 mIU/L; creatinine 62 micromol/L; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m^2
data_table.History: Bipolar I; two prior manic episodes inpatient; lithium 1000 mg for 4 years; planned pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her mood stabiliser?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for pregnancy and arrange a foetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks to screen for anomalies
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy because of a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation and a further 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment; it is never a substitute for lithium in a pregnant woman (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch to lamotrigine 200 mg daily as it has the safest teratogenic profile of the mood stabilisers with regular perinatal psychiatry review through pregnancy and the postnatal period
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is safer in pregnancy but is less effective at preventing manic episodes; switching from an effective lithium regimen in a woman with prior manic episodes risks relapse and is not first line (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy).

options.text: Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose, arrange a foetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks and monitor levels through pregnancy and continue perinatal psychiatric review through pregnancy and the postnatal period
options.rationale: In a woman with severe bipolar I disorder and prior manic episodes, the risk of postpartum relapse without a mood stabiliser is around 50 percent and outweighs the small absolute increase in Ebstein anomaly risk with lithium (about 6 per 1000 versus 1 per 1000 baseline); the RANZCP advice is to continue at the lowest effective dose with a foetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks and level monitoring through pregnancy (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease lithium during the first trimester only and reintroduce it at 14 weeks after organogenesis is complete and continue perinatal psychiatry review through pregnancy and the postnatal period
options.rationale: Discontinuation of lithium during the first trimester exposes the woman to a high risk of relapse and does not eliminate cardiac teratogenicity risk; consistent continuation with monitoring is safer than intermittent stopping (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy).

options.text: Add olanzapine 10 mg orally at night while ceasing lithium to avoid any teratogenicity risk and continue perinatal psychiatry review throughout the pregnancy and the postnatal period
options.rationale: Olanzapine is a reasonable alternative to lithium but replacing an effective lithium regimen introduces its own metabolic risks and gestational diabetes risk without meaningful reduction in overall teratogenicity risk; the risk versus benefit favours continuing lithium in a woman with two prior manic episodes (Source: RANZCP mood disorders in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: In a woman with bipolar I disorder and prior manic episodes the risk of postpartum psychosis or mania is around 50 percent without prophylactic mood stabilisation, so continuation of lithium in pregnancy is often justified. The absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly with first trimester lithium exposure is around 6 per 1000 births compared with 1 per 1000 in the general population, an increase that is small relative to the relapse risk of stopping the drug. Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy because of its high risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental impairment. Continuation of lithium is accompanied by more frequent level monitoring due to increased renal clearance and a foetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks.
key_points: Ebstein risk about 6 per 1000 versus 1 per 1000 baseline with first trimester lithium.
Postpartum relapse risk about 50 percent without a mood stabiliser in bipolar I disorder.
Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy the volume of distribution and renal clearance of lithium change, so serum lithium levels are checked monthly until 34 weeks and then weekly, with the dose held on the day of delivery to avoid postpartum toxicity.
